# Lists That Do What You Mean {#chp:lists}

R is generous with partial matching. Type `z$a` and R will happily hand you
`z$aaa`, without a word of complaint. Most of the time that is a convenience.
Sometimes it is a bug that waits quietly until the worst moment. This chapter
gives you lists and attributes that refuse to guess.

## Stop `$` from guessing {#sec:strict-list}

You want `$` to return only exact name matches. Use `strict_list()` to build
such a list:

```{r}
library(xfun)

z = strict_list(aaa = "I am aaa", b = 1:5)
z$a    # NULL: no partial match
z$aaa  # the element you asked for
```

Partial matching is switched off for this list, so `z$a` comes back empty
instead of pretending to be `aaa`.

## Make an existing list strict {#sec:as-strict}

Maybe the list came from someone else's code, and you cannot change how it was
built. `as_strict_list()` converts it for you. Here is the trap, first:

```{r}
z = strict_list(aaa = "I am aaa", b = 1:5)
z2 = unclass(z)  # back to an ordinary list
z2$a             # "I am aaa": partial match fires
```

And the fix:

```{r}
z3 = as_strict_list(z2)
z3$a  # NULL again
```

## Stop `attr()` from guessing {#sec:attr2}

Attributes have the same problem, because `attr()` also matches partial names.
`attr2()` is an alias for `attr(exact = TRUE)`, so it only matches what you
spell out:

```{r}
x = structure(list(), foobar = 42)
base::attr(x, "foo")  # 42: partial match
attr2(x, "foo")       # NULL
attr2(x, "foobar")    # 42
```

Use `attr2()` by default in your own code and you will skip a whole class of
head-scratching moments.
